Enantioselective Synthesis of Multifunctionalized 4 H‑Pyrans via
Formal [4 + 2] Annulation Process by Bifunctional Phosphonium Salt
Catalysis
Jia-Hong Wu, † Jianke Pan, † Juan Du, † Xiaoxia Wang, † Xuemei Wang, † Chunhui Jiang, †,‡
and Tianli Wang *,†
†Key Laboratory of Green Chemistry & Technology of Ministry of Education, College of Chemistry, Sichuan University, Chengdu
610064, P. R. China
‡School of Environmental and Chemical Engineering, Jiangsu University of Science and Technology, 2 Mengxi Road, Zhenjiang
212003, P. R. China
*S Supporting Information
ABSTRACT: A highly enantioselective formal [4 + 2]
annulation involving electron-de ﬁcient allenes as C2-synthons
has been developed under bifunctional phosphonium salt
catalysis. With this catalytic protocol, a wide range of
synthetically interesting and highly functionalized chiral 4 H-
pyran derivatives were readily prepared in good yields (up to
99%) with outstanding diastereo- and enantioselectivities (up
to >20:1 dr, up to >99.9% ee). The utility and the practicality
of this method were demonstrated by the gram-scale reaction
and facile elaboration. Of note, this is the ﬁrst example of an
asymmetric annulation reaction involving allenic reactants
under a phase-transfer catalysis system.
I
n the past decades, asymmetric PTC (phase transfer
catalysis) has been known as a kind of rather powerful
and e ﬃcient method for enantioselective preparation of
structurally diverse and synthetically useful molecular
architectures, and a number of quaternary ammonium salts
have been commonly applied in PTC. 1 In contrast, asymmetric
reactions catalyzed by chiral phosphonium salts are rare and
still underdeveloped.
2 The pioneering works were recently
conducted by the research groups of Ooi 3 and Maruoka. 4
Lately, Ma and co-workers disclosed a binol-derived P-spiro-
phosphonium salt and applied it to an asymmetric amination
reaction.
5 More recently, Zhao 6 and Lu 7 developed a few
phosphonium salt catalysts derived from natural amino acids
and further preliminarily realized their utilization in asym-
metric conjugate addition and substitution reactions. Our
group recently achieved enantioselective annulation reactions
by designing and making use of novel dipeptide-based
bifunctional phosphonium salt catalysts.
8 It must be noted
that such type of bifunctional phosphonium salts is highly
tunable, but their application in asymmetric organic synthesis
is still rare.
On the other hand, electron-de ﬁcient allenes containing
highly activated C C bonds have been widely employed in
asymmetric organic synthesis, especially in a wide range of
asymmetric cyclization processes by a phosphine 9,10 or
amine11−13 catalysis system. However, their use in a phase
transfer catalysis (PTC) system has been rather limited. 14 To
our best knowledge, there are just two examples achieved by
chiral ammonium salt catalysis ( Figure 1a). In 2008, Jørgensen
et al. utilized cyclic β-ketoesters and glycine imine derivatives
as pronucleophiles in a conjugated addition with electron-
deﬁcient allenes by ammonium salt catalysis. 14a In 2013,
Maruoka and co-workers di sclosed an ammonium salt-
catalyzed asymmetric alkylation and alleno-Mannich-type
reaction of 1-alkylallene-1,3-dicarboxylates. 14b Consequently,
developing other types of reactions involving allenic esters by
PTC is highly desirable. In continuation of our major interest
in bifunctional organocatalysis involving phosphonium salt
catalysts, we questioned whether activated allenes could be
eﬃciently used as C2/C3 synthons for an annulation process,
in combination with α,β-unsaturated ketones as C4 synthons
to produce structurally unique and biologically signi ﬁcant
cyclic compounds ( Scheme 1 ).15 In this report, we described
an asymmetric [4 + 2] annulation reaction involving allenes as
C2-synthons for the synthesis of highly functionalized 4 H-
pyrans under a bifunctional phosphonium salt catalysis system
(Figure 1 b).
Initially, we began our studies via investigating the
annulation reactions between 3-alkenyl-oxindole 1a and allenic
ester 2a in the presence of a number of amino acid derived
bifunctional phosphonium salt catalysts ( Table 1 ). L-Valine-

for promoting this transformation to produce 4 H-pyran 3a in

Changing the backbone to alanine, tert-leucine, or threonine
did not improve the enantioselectivities (entries 6 −8). While
the

dramatically (entries 9 and 10), and the catalyst P
10 tuned out

3PO4 was
the optimal choice of base and the xylene was the suitable
solvent (entries 12 and 13).
16 Indeed, the reaction also worked
well with 10 mol % catalyst, a ﬀording the corresponding
product in 98% yield and 93% ee (entry 14). Practically, there
is no reaction when the base is absent (entry 15).
With the optimal reaction conditions in hand ( Table 1, entry
14), we started to focus our attention on the scope of this [4 +
2] annulation between 3-alkenyl-oxindoles 1 and allenic ester 2
(Table 2). The ester substituents and N-protected groups of 3-
alkenyl-oxindoles were ﬁrst investigated. Pleasantly, various
ester groups (EWG
1) on the 3-alkenyl-oxindoles were well
tolerated, furnishing the corresponding products ( 3a−f)i n
excellent yields (90 −98%) with good to excellent stereo-
selectivities (all >20:1 dr,8 6 −99% ee). N-Benzyloxycarbonyl
3-alkenyl-oxindole was also compatible to deliver the expected
product 3g in high yield (88%) with high stereoselectivities
(>20:1 dr and 84% ee). Subsequently, various 3-alkenyl-
oxindoles bearing electron-withdrawing, -donating, and -
neutral groups on the phenyl ring were found to be compatible
under the standard reaction conditions, and the products 3h−y
were produced in high yields (70 −99%) with excellent
diastereo- and enantioselectivities (all >20:1 dr,8 5 −96% ee).
Of note, when the benzene rings bore electron-withdrawing
substituents, the yields of annulation products were slightly
lowered ( 3m, 3s, and 3y). The catalytic reactions also worked
well when di ﬀerent allenic esters were employed, giving the
expected products 4a−e in high yields (88 −98%) with
excellent stereoselectivities (all >20:1 dr and 80 −93% ee).

Subsequently, we also investigated the [4 + 2] annulation
between ketone-substituted 3-alkenyl-oxindoles and electron-
deﬁcient allenes ( Table 3 ). Generally, a wide range of ketone-
activated 3-alkenyl-oxindoles ( 5) with di ﬀerent substituents in
the para-, ortho-, or meta-position on the phenyl ring of ketone-
moiety proceeded rather well to deliver the desirable products
6a−j in high yields (75 −98%) with excellent stereoselectivities
(up to >20:1 dr and 93 −98% ee). When the N-protection
group was changed to Cbz, the reaction also proceeded
smoothly ( 6k). Moreover, n-butyl-substituted allenoate also
proved to be an excellent substrate and a ﬀorded the product 6l
with an exceptionally high ee value of greater than 99.9% with
92% yield. Moreover, some g ram-scale reactions were
conducted to prepare the desirable products such as 3b and
3l with comparable yields as well as excellent diastereose-
lectivities and enantioselectivities ( Figure S2a ); further, the
product 3l was readily transformed into di ﬀerent optically
enriched compounds 7 and 8 in high yields ( Figure S2b ).
16
Based on the obtained results and our previous explora-
tions,8 a plausible mechanism was presented in Figure 2 a. We
propose that the base-mediated deprotonation process initially
occurs to generate the anionic intermediate A/B. Then, α-
addition of this intermediate A/B to 3-alkenyl-oxindoles ( 1)
leads to the key intermediate anionic C which may be
stabilized by a phosphonium cation via ion-pair interaction.
Intramolecular β-addition of C yields the intermediate D
which can isomerize to form main intermediate E. Last, the
anionic intermediate E abstracts a proton from the system to
generate the desired product 3 and simultaneously release the
phosphonium salt catalyst, which will enter the reaction cycle
again. Accordingly, the deuterium-labeling experiment was
performed to gain some preliminary insight into this catalytic
cycle. When 3.0 equiv of D
2O were added into the standard
reaction system, deuterium incorporation into the α′-position
of product ( d-3b) was observed, which suggests the bene ﬁcial
existence of intermediate E in the catalytic cycle. To gain some
insights into the origin of the stereochemical outcome, we
further prepared the methylated catalyst P
10‑1 and tested its
catalytic ability for the model reaction. It was found that either
the enantioselectivity decre ased dramatically or racemic
product was delivered in the absence of a chiral catalyst

(Figure 2c, entries 1 −3). Moreover, the phosphonium chloride
catalyst ( P10‑2) still worked well for a ﬀording desired 3b
(Figure 2 c, entry 4). When the reaction was conducted in
methanol, the result was messy. Of note, the reaction could not
occur when no base was added ( Figure 2 c, entry 6). These
experimental results indicated that the weak-bond interactions,
such as those related to ion pairs and H-bonding, were critical
for the excellent stereoselectivities under such a bifunctional
phosphonium system ( Figure S3 ).
16
In summary, an e ﬃcient alternative for the enantioselective
synthesis of highly functionalized 4 H-pyrans via bifunctional
phosphonium salt catalyzed [4 + 2] annulation of electron-
deﬁcient allenes with 3-alkenyl-oxindoles has been disclosed.
With this catalytic asymmetric protocol, a broad range of
highly substituted 4 H-pyran derivatives were prepared in high
yields with excellent diastereo- and enatioselectivities under
mild reaction conditions. These results indicated that this kind
of structurally tunable bifunctional phosphonium salt catalysis
was a practicable strategy to construct structurally complicated
chiral compounds, and further investigation is ongoing in our
laboratory.

evidence.text:
Enantioselective Synthesis of Multifunctionalized 4 H‑Pyrans via
Formal [4 + 2] Annulation Process by Bifunctional Phosphonium Salt
Catalysis
Jia-Hong Wu, † Jianke Pan, † Juan Du, † Xiaoxia Wang, † Xuemei Wang, † Chunhui Jiang, †,‡
and Tianli Wang *,†
†Key Laboratory of Green Chemistry & Technology of Ministry of Education, College of Chemistry, Sichuan University, Chengdu
610064, P. R. China
‡School of Environmental and Chemical Engineering, Jiangsu University of Science and Technology, 2 Mengxi Road, Zhenjiang
212003, P. R. China
*S Supporting Information
ABSTRACT: A highly enantioselective formal [4 + 2]
annulation involving electron-de ﬁcient allenes as C2-synthons
has been developed under bifunctional phosphonium salt
catalysis. With this catalytic protocol, a wide range of
synthetically interesting and highly functionalized chiral 4 H-
pyran derivatives were readily prepared in good yields (up to
99%) with outstanding diastereo- and enantioselectivities (up
to >20:1 dr, up to >99.9% ee). The utility and the practicality
of this method were demonstrated by the gram-scale reaction
and facile elaboration. Of note, this is the ﬁrst example of an
asymmetric annulation reaction involving allenic reactants
under a phase-transfer catalysis system.
I
n the past decades, asymmetric PTC (phase transfer
catalysis) has been known as a kind of rather powerful
and e ﬃcient method for enantioselective preparation of
structurally diverse and synthetically useful molecular
architectures, and a number of quaternary ammonium salts
have been commonly applied in PTC. 1 In contrast, asymmetric
reactions catalyzed by chiral phosphonium salts are rare and
still underdeveloped.
2 The pioneering works were recently

In summary, an e ﬃcient alternative for the enantioselective
synthesis of highly functionalized 4 H-pyrans via bifunctional
phosphonium salt catalyzed [4 + 2] annulation of electron-
deﬁcient allenes with 3-alkenyl-oxindoles has been disclosed.
With this catalytic asymmetric protocol, a broad range of
highly substituted 4 H-pyran derivatives were prepared in high
yields with excellent diastereo- and enatioselectivities under
mild reaction conditions. These results indicated that this kind
of structurally tunable bifunctional phosphonium salt catalysis
was a practicable strategy to construct structurally complicated
chiral compounds, and further investigation is ongoing in our
laboratory.
